Rani of Jhansi: Prominent leader of the 1857 Indian rebellion.
A U.S. attorney general turned New York senator, this icon of American liberalism was assassinated in 1968 — and his brothers John and Ted were no strangers to office either. Who is he?
Robert F. Kennedy: American politician and lawyer (1925–1968)
A career diplomat turned politician, this BJP member rose from foreign secretary to become India's longest-serving minister to hold the External Affairs portfolio exclusively. Who is he?
S. Jaishankar: Indian diplomat and politician (born 1955)
Dominating the Pontic steppe from the 5th century BC to the 4th century AD, this confederation of ancient Iranian horse nomads formed part of the wider Scythian world — who were they?
Sarmatians: Large Iranian confederation that existed in classical antiquity.

Spurned in childhood as an illegitimate son, this early-19th-century monarch transformed his kingdom's army into a formidable fighting force during his reign from 1816 to 1828 — who was this Southern African king?
Shaka: Zulu king from 1816 to 1828. King Shaka was born in the lunar month of uNtulikazi (July) in 1787, in Mthonjaneni, KwaZulu-Natal Province, South Africa.
Stepping up from hostess for her assassinated husband, this Sri Lankan politician became, in 1960, the first woman in the world elected prime minister — who was she?
Sirimavo Bandaranaike: Prime Minister of Sri Lanka (1916–2000)
Released from Dutch detention by invading Japanese forces in WWII, this nationalist leader went on to become the very first president of his newly independent nation. Who is he?
Sukarno: President of Indonesia from 1945 to 1967.
This brief conflict ran from June 27 to July 7, 1991, ending when the Brioni Accords settled Slovenia's break from Yugoslavia — what was it called?

Ten-Day War: 1991 Slovenia-Yugoslavia conflict. It was fought between the Slovenian Territorial Defence and the Slovenian National Police Force on one side, and the Yugoslav People's Army on the other.
Before ruling Rome from 79 to 81 AD, he commanded the siege that ended the Jewish rebellion — and became the first Roman emperor ever to directly succeed his own biological father; who was he?
Titus: Roman emperor from AD 79 to 81. Titus Flavius Vespasianus (30 December 39 – 13 September 81 AD) was Roman emperor from 79 to 81 AD.

Centered on the Armenian highlands between three great lakes and locked in frequent wars with Assyria, this Iron Age kingdom left behind cuneiform inscriptions and massive fortresses before falling to the Medes or Cyrus the Great — what kingdom was it?
Urartu: Iron-Age kingdom of the ancient Near East.
Leading Russia's Liberal Democratic Party from 1992 until his death in 2022, this firebrand ran in nearly every presidential election and openly called for military action against NATO — who is he?
Once a loyal Nazi admiral running Germany's military intelligence service, he turned to sabotage and resistance against Hitler — and was hanged for treason at Flossenbürg in 1945. Who was he?

After his father — a former Andhra Pradesh chief minister — died in a 2009 helicopter crash, this politician toured the state on a consoling 'Odarpu Yatra' before founding his own party and later becoming chief minister himself — who is he?

Y. S. Jagan Mohan Reddy: Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh, India. Jagan Mohan Reddy started his political career in the Indian National Congress and was elected as the Member of Parliament of Kadapa in 2009.
Pakistan's longest-serving de-facto ruler, this general seized power in a 1977 coup and held it until his death in a 1988 airplane crash — who is he?
Zia-ul-Haq: 6th President of Pakistan from 1978 to 1988.
Which of these four was born earliest?
John Ray (born 1627) is the earliest of the four. John Ray (29 November 1627 – 17 January 1705) was an English Christian naturalist and one of the earliest English parson-naturalists.
Which of these four was born earliest?
Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four. Henry Vaughan (1621 – 23 April 1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet, author and translator writing in English, and a medical physician.
Which of these four began earliest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as a physicist?
John Theophilus Desaguliers is a physicist. Desaguliers's most important patron was James Brydges, 1st Duke of Chandos.
Which of these four is a chemist?
Otto Hahn is a chemist. Otto Hahn (German: [ˈɔtoː ˈhaːn]; 8 March 1879 – 28 July 1968) was a German chemist who was a pioneer in the field of radiochemistry.
What is the atomic number of Californium?
Californium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Cf and atomic number 98.
In what year was Mohamed Atta born?
Mohamed Atta: In Hamburg, Atta attended prayers at the al-Quds Mosque where he met Marwan al-Shehhi, Ramzi bin al-Shibh, and Ziad Jarrah, with whom he formed the Hamburg cell.
In what year was Rakesh Sharma born?
Rakesh Sharma (born 13 January 1949) is an Indian cosmonaut and a pilot of the Indian Air Force.
In what year was Mikhail Lomonosov born?
Mikhail Lomonosov: One of the founders of modern geology, Lomonosov was also a poet and influenced the formation of the modern Russian literary language.
In what year did Hamish Harding die?
Hamish Harding: George Hamish Livingston Harding (24 June 1964 – 18 June 2023) was a British businessman, pilot and adventurer based in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
In what year did Manmohan Singh die?
Manmohan Singh: A member of the Indian National Congress, Singh was the first and remains the only Sikh prime minister of India.
In what year was Plutonium discovered?
Plutonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Pu and atomic number 94.
In what year was Tungsten discovered?
Tungsten (also called wolfram) is a chemical element; it has symbol W (from German: Wolfram) and atomic number 74.
Ilyushin Il-96: Voronezh Aircraft Production Association. It is powered by four high-bypass Aviadvigatel PS-90 twin-spool turbofan engines.
In which country is Dassault Mirage 2000?
Dassault Mirage 2000: France. Work on what would become the Mirage 2000 originated with the "Delta 1000" project launched in 1972.
Who is credited with discovering Horologium?

Horologium (constellation): Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. It was first described by the French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in 1756 and visualized by him as a clock with a pendulum and a second hand.
Who is credited with discovering Hubble's law?
Hubble's law: Georges Lemaître. The Friedmann equations showed the universe might be expanding, and presented the expansion speed if that were the case.
Who is credited with discovering Eris?
Eris (dwarf planet): Michael E. Brown. Eris (minor-planet number 136199) is the most massive and second-largest known dwarf planet in the Solar System.
Hiding in coffee, fresh bread, and ripe fruit, this aldehyde is also what your liver makes when breaking down alcohol — and a prime culprit behind the morning-after hangover. What is it?
Acetaldehyde (IUPAC systematic name ethanal) is an organic chemical compound with the formula CH3CH=O.
This exaggerated immune reaction causes the body to mistake a harmless substance for a threat, triggering symptoms from a runny nose to a full anaphylactic reaction — what is it?
Allergy is an exaggerated immune response where the body mistakenly identifies an ordinarily harmless allergen as a threat.
Nicknamed the 'nail mosquito,' this genus — first classified in 1818 — is the sole mosquito genus known to carry human malaria — which genus is it?
Anopheles is a genus of mosquito first described by the German entomologist J. W. Meigen in 1818.
This medical condition, most often caused in the developed world by liver cirrhosis, is the abnormal buildup of fluid within the abdominal cavity — what is it called?
Ascites is the abnormal build-up of fluid in the abdomen.

Ranking among the largest wild cats, this population of the Panthera tigris tigris subspecies has roamed the Indian subcontinent since the Late Pleistocene and is found from India to southwestern China — name it?
Bengal tiger is a population of the Panthera tigris tigris subspecies. It is distributed from India, southern Nepal, Bangladesh, Bhutan to Southwestern China.

This semi-solid tissue inside the spongy portions of bones serves as the primary site of new blood cell production in birds and mammals, making up roughly 5% of an adult human's body mass — what tissue is it?
Bone marrow is a semi-solid tissue found within the spongy (also known as cancellous) portions of bones.

What suborder of orthopteran insects — its Latin name meaning 'chisel-bearing,' after the stout shape of its members' egg-laying organs — includes grasshoppers, ground-hoppers, and pygmy mole crickets?
Caelifera are a suborder of orthopteran insects. The latter should not be confused with the mole crickets (Gryllotalpidae), which belong to the other Orthopteran suborder Ensifera.

Derived from the amino acid tyrosine and fifty percent bound to plasma proteins in your bloodstream, what class of neurotransmitter has a benzene ring topped with two hydroxyl groups plus a side-chain amine?

Catecholamine (abbreviated CA), most typically a 3,4-dihydroxyphenethylamine, is a monoamine neurotransmitter, an organic compound that has a catechol (benzene with two hydroxyl side groups next to each other) and a side-chain amine.
Most species of this loud insect superfamily emerge annually, but a few North American ones famously emerge en masse only once every several years. What insects are they?
Cicada are a superfamily, the Cicadoidea, of insects in the order Hemiptera (true bugs).
Known by a colorful nickname, this inflammation of the clear layer over the white of the eye turns it pink, may leave it stuck shut by morning, and spreads easily — what is it?
Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the thin and clear layer that covers the white surface of the eye and the inner eyelid.
A law professor known for scholarship on retribution and criminal sentencing, this Harvard-trained academic was killed in 2014 in a murder-for-hire scheme linked to a custody dispute — who is he?

Dan Markel (October 9, 1972 - July 19, 2014) was a Canadian-born attorney and law professor who wrote various works on retribution in criminal law and sentencing with a focus on the role of punishment in the criminal justice system.
A member of the catecholamine family made by stripping a carboxyl group from L-DOPA, this brain chemical is central to reward-motivated behavior — what is it?
Dopamine (DA, a contraction of 3,4-dihydroxyphenethylamine) is a neuromodulatory molecule that plays several important roles in cells.
In this lung disease, the walls between tiny air sacs break down into fewer, larger spaces, shrinking the surface available for gas exchange and starving the blood of oxygen. What condition?
Emphysema is a condition of the lung marked by abnormal enlargement of the alveoli with loss of pulmonary elasticity.
Despite its name, this highly sociable oceanic dolphin earned its label from a skull resembling the orca's — it can reach 20 feet and even forms mixed pods with bottlenose dolphins. What is it?
False killer whale (Pseudorca crassidens) is a species of oceanic dolphin that is the only extant representative of the genus Pseudorca.
He worked on uranium enrichment during the Manhattan Project, then — after McCarthyism cost him his physics post — founded San Francisco's hands-on Exploratorium museum; who was he?

Frank Oppenheimer (August 14, 1912 - February 3, 1985) was an American particle physicist, cattle rancher, professor of physics at the University of Colorado, and the founder of the Exploratorium in San Francisco.

A 1946 civilian demonstrator version of this British fighter became the world's first civilian-registered jet aircraft, decades after it debuted as the Allies' sole combat jet of World War II — which aircraft?
Gloster Meteor was the first British jet fighter and the Allies' only jet aircraft to engage in combat operations during the Second World War.
The first Professor of the Public Understanding of Mathematics at Cambridge, she's also a BBC broadcaster who explores the math behind human relationships — who is she?
Hannah Fry (born 21 February 1984) is a British mathematician, author and broadcaster.
This common household insect, likely originating in the Middle East, mates only once in her lifetime but stores the sperm to fertilize repeated batches of about 100 eggs — what insect is it?
Housefly (Musca domestica) is a fly of the suborder Cyclorrhapha.
Once extracted from the leaves of Indigofera plants and now mostly made synthetically, this insoluble blue colorant is famous for dyeing denim and enabling tricks like stone washing. What is it?
Indigo dye is an organic compound with a distinctive blue color.
Enlisting as a valet named 'Jean' on Bougainville's expedition, this expert botanist disguised herself as a man and became the first woman to sail all the way around the globe — who was she?

Jeanne Baret (27 July 1740 - 5 August 1807) was a French explorer, naturalist, and botanist who is recognised as the first woman to have completed a voyage of circumnavigation of the globe, which she did via boat.
Native to eastern and southern Africa, this flowering shrub is the sole species in its genus and has a documented history of cultivation dating back to Ethiopia's Harar region. Name the plant?
Khat (Catha edulis), also known as Bushman's tea, especially in South Africa, is a species of flowering plant in the family Celastraceae, and the sole species in genus Catha.
Sometimes a side effect of medication or an alcohol interaction, which state of sluggishness and low motivation usually resolves with rest and better nutrition?
Lethargy is a state of physical or mental weariness, fatigue, sluggishness, or lack of energy.
This paired organ, located near the backbone on either side of the heart in most mammals, extracts oxygen from the air and releases carbon dioxide back into it — name the organ?
Lung are the primary organs of the respiratory system in many animals, including humans.

In 1895 this American psychologist completed every requirement for a Harvard Ph.D., only to be refused the degree because of her gender — yet she still invented the paired-associate learning technique. Who was she?
Mary Whiton Calkins (30 March 1863 - 26 February 1930) was an American philosopher and psychologist, whose work informed theory and research of memory, dreams and the self.
Entering Soviet service in 1983 alongside the larger Su-27, this 'Fulcrum' air-superiority fighter was later adapted into a multirole jet — which aircraft is it?
Mikoyan MiG-29 (NATO reporting name: Fulcrum) is a twin-engine fighter aircraft designed in the Soviet Union.
Lacking a cell wall entirely, this tiny bacterial species causes a form of atypical lung infection linked to cold agglutinin disease — which microbe first isolated as the 1944 'Eaton agent'?
Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a species of very small-cell bacteria that lack a cell wall, in the class Mollicutes.
Doubling as a hormone, neurotransmitter, and neuromodulator, this catecholamine's very name nods to the kidney — and goes by 'noradrenaline' nearly everywhere outside the United States. What is it?

Norepinephrine (NE), also called noradrenaline (NA) or noradrenalin, is an organic chemical in the catecholamine family that functions in the brain and body as a hormone, neurotransmitter and neuromodulator.
Often silent at first, this disease arises from an ovary or nearby structures and announces itself only later with bloating, pelvic pain, and abdominal swelling — what is it?
Ovarian cancer is a cancerous tumor of an ovary.
It comes in a G version for the needle and a V version for the mouth, and it owes its name to the very mould it's coaxed from — which medication?
Penicillin (PCN or PEN) are a group of beta-lactam antibiotics originally obtained from Penicillium moulds, principally P. chrysogenum.
Native to South America and the most economically important member of the Bromeliaceae family, this tropical 'multiple fruit' became a 17th-century European symbol of luxury — what is it?
Pineapple (Ananas comosus) is a tropical plant with an edible fruit; it is the most economically significant plant in the family Bromeliaceae.

Native to North American grasslands, these burrowing, herbivorous ground squirrels come in five species, black-tailed, white-tailed, Gunnison's, Utah, and Mexican. Name this genus, Cynomys, by its common two-word name?
Prairie dog (genus Cynomys) are herbivorous burrowing ground squirrels native to the grasslands of North America.
This white, odorless nitroamine explosive, widely used since World War II, is the explosive agent inside C-4 plastic explosive — what is it called?
RDX (Research Department Explosive or Royal Demolition Explosive), or hexogen, also known by other names, is an organic compound with the formula (CH2N2O2)3.
A Jesuit priest, poet, and diplomat from the Republic of Ragusa, this polymath produced an early precursor of atomic theory and in 1753 discovered the Moon has no atmosphere — who was he?
Roger Joseph Boscovich (18 May 1711 - 13 February 1787) was a physicist, astronomer, mathematician, philosopher, diplomat, poet, theologian, Jesuit priest, and a polymath from the Republic of Ragusa.

Sitting near the center of the Milky Way between Libra and Sagittarius, this zodiac constellation's recognition predates Greek civilization, and it was among the 48 catalogued by Ptolemy in the second century — what's the constellation?
Scorpius is a zodiac constellation located in the Southern celestial hemisphere, where it sits near the center of the Milky Way, between Libra to the west and Sagittarius to the east.
Typically a bony enclosure around a vertebrate's brain, though cartilage in some fish and amphibians, this head structure combines a neurocranium with a facial skeleton — name it?

Skull is typically a bony enclosure around the brain of a vertebrate. In a human, the skull comprises two prominent parts: the neurocranium and the facial skeleton, which evolved from the first pharyngeal arch.
Named from the Greek word for tallow, this soft waxy 18-carbon saturated fatty compound is common in animal fats like beef tallow and lard — what is it called?
Stearic acid (stee-) is a saturated fatty acid with an 18-carbon chain.
This genus of flowering plants in the daisy family is better known by the fluffy-seeded lawn weed it produces, with two European species now invasive nearly worldwide. What is it?
Taraxacum is a genus of flowering plants in the family Asteraceae which consists of species commonly known as dandelions.
Joining a tech giant in 1998 to run worldwide operations, this executive served as its COO before stepping up to CEO the day Steve Jobs resigned in 2011 — who is he?
Tim Cook (born November 1, 1960) is an American business executive who has served as the chief executive officer (CEO) of Apple since 2011.
Lined with a type of tissue called transitional epithelium, this narrow tube can develop kidney stones or reflux problems and connects each kidney to the bladder — what is it?
Ureter are tubes composed of smooth muscle that transport urine from the kidneys to the urinary bladder.
He co-developed the V-2 at Peenemünde — the first artificial object to cross the Kármán line into space — before bringing his rocketry to the United States; who was this engineer?
Wernher von Braun (23 March 1912 - 16 June 1977) was a German American aerospace engineer and space architect.
Also called motor neuron disease or Lou Gehrig's disease, this terminal condition progressively destroys the neurons that control voluntary muscle movement — what is it?
Nicknamed the painted hunter for its mottled coat, this sub-Saharan canine hunts cooperatively at dawn and dusk and is the only living member of its genus, Lycaon — which species?
African wild dog: Species of canine. The African wild dog (Lycaon pictus), also called painted dog and Cape hunting dog, is a wild canine native to sub-Saharan Africa.
With more than 1,100 species including onions, garlic, leeks, and chives, this is the largest genus in the flowering plant family Amaryllidaceae — which genus?
Allium: Genus of flowering plants. The flowers form an umbel at the top of a leafless stalk.
This cosmopolitan family of water birds, found on every continent but Antarctica, groups together the ducks, geese, and swans — what is it?
Anatidae: Biological family of water birds. The family has a cosmopolitan distribution, occurring on all the world's continents except Antarctica.
Lacking a tail due to a mutation in the TBXT gene, this superfamily of primates includes gibbons as the 'lesser' branch and humans among the 'great' branch — which animal group?
Ape: Superfamily of primates. The family Hylobatidae, the lesser apes, include four genera and a total of 20 species of gibbon, including the lar gibbon and the siamang, all native to Asia.
First described in 1740 under the name Compositae, this enormous flowering-plant family includes daisies, asters and sunflowers — what is it?
Asteraceae: Large family of flowering plants.
A sessile marine arthropod related to crabs and lobsters, folklore once claimed geese hatched fully formed from one variety of it — what creature is it?
Barnacle: Subclass of sessile marine crustaceans.
Also called the bearcat, this dark, shaggy, tree-dwelling Asian viverrid sports a prehensile tail and musk glands that famously smell of buttered popcorn — what is it?
Binturong: Asian mammal also known as a bearcat.
Developed from a wide-body airliner and selected in 2011 to replace an aging fleet of aerial tankers, this refueling aircraft entered US Air Force service in 2019 — which aircraft?
Boeing KC-46 Pegasus: American military aerial refueling and transport aircraft.
Native to Australia and naturally green and yellow with black scalloped markings, this small, long-tailed parrot is one of the world's most popular pet birds — what is it?
Encompassing wolves, dogs, coyotes, and golden jackals, which genus is defined by its members' massive skulls, long legs, and comparatively short ears and tails?
Canis: Genus of canines. Canis is a genus of the Caninae which includes multiple extant species, such as wolves, dogs, coyotes, and golden jackals.
This mint-family herb, described by Carl Linnaeus in 1753, takes its common name from its long historical association with cats — which plant?
Catnip: Nepeta cataria; species of plant.
Her famous experiment proved parity is not conserved — earning Lee and Yang the 1957 Nobel while she received the inaugural Wolf Prize in Physics instead. Which Manhattan Project physicist was she?
Sold under the brand name Anafranil, this tricyclic antidepressant treats obsessive-compulsive disorder but also premature ejaculation and the cataplexy that comes with narcolepsy — which drug?
Clomipramine: Antidepressant. It has also been notably used to treat premature ejaculation and the cataplexy associated with narcolepsy.
Once classified among the thrushes, this small Old World flycatcher was later reassigned to the family Muscicapidae — which bird?
Common redstart: Species of bird. The common redstart (Phoenicurus phoenicurus), or often simply redstart, is a small passerine bird in the genus Phoenicurus.
This interdisciplinary field draws on sociology, psychology, and law to study crime, deviant behavior, and the workings of the justice system — what is it called?
Criminology: Field of studies related to crimes.
At just 37 this American biologist won a 1975 Nobel for discovering reverse transcriptase, later running Caltech and founding the Whitehead Institute — who is he?
David Baltimore: American biologist and Nobel laureate (1938–2025)
These warmblooded reptiles ruled the land for the whole Mesozoic, and one feathered lineage of theirs survived the extinction 66 million years ago as today's birds — what group is this?
Dinosaur: Clade of reptiles. Since then, mounted fossil dinosaur skeletons have been major attractions at museums worldwide, and dinosaurs have become an enduring part of popular culture.
Belonging to the phylum Annelida and often called a 'nightcrawler' by anglers, this segmented soil-dweller is the classic bait fished from underground burrows — which invertebrate?
Continuous with the outer nuclear membrane and absent from red blood cells, this organelle comes in rough and smooth forms and handles protein folding — what is it?
Endoplasmic reticulum: Cell organelle that processes proteins.
Recognizable by its striking yellow-and-azure plumage, this small European songbird nests in tree holes and can acrobatically hang upside-down from branch tips — which bird?
Eurasian blue tit: Species of bird. The Eurasian blue tit (Cyanistes caeruleus) is a small passerine bird in the tit family, Paridae.

Colloquially called squirting or gushing, this fluid is expelled from the Skene's gland near the urethra around the time of orgasm — and researchers stress it's physiologically distinct from coital incontinence. What is it?
Female ejaculation: Expulsion of fluid during orgasm.
This double-layered fold of skin covering the glans is attached by an elastic band called the frenulum and is typically fused in place at birth — what is it?
Foreskin: Retractable fold of skin which covers and protects the glans of the penis.
Often triggered by H. pylori infection or NSAID use, this inflammation of the stomach lining can, in its autoimmune form, lead to pernicious anemia — what condition is it?
Gastritis: Inflammation of the stomach lining. It may occur as a short episode or have a long duration.

The only Allied jet aircraft to see combat in World War II, this British fighter entered service with No. 616 Squadron RAF in July 1944, powered by engines pioneered by Frank Whittle — which aircraft?
Gloster Meteor: Britain's first jet fighter, 1943–1980s.
This motorsport engineer led the Haas Formula One team from 2016 to 2023 before becoming CEO of a MotoGP outfit — who is he?
Guenther Steiner: Italian and American motor racing engineer (born 1965)
Despite common nicknames like 'Christmas rose' and 'Lenten rose,' this poisonous Eurasian flowering genus isn't actually related to roses at all — what is it?
Discovered in 2013 in South Africa's Rising Star Cave system, this small-brained archaic human species yielded over 1,500 bone specimens from at least 15 individuals — which species?
Homo naledi: South African archaic human species. The initial discovery comprises 1,550 specimens of bone, representing 737 different skeletal elements, and at least 15 different individuals.
A person with this condition becomes unduly alarmed by even the most minor symptom, convinced a serious illness is upon them despite no medical diagnosis — what is it?
Hypochondriasis: Excessive fear of developing illness.
This cerebrovascular condition is a localized ballooning of a brain blood vessel most often found in the Circle of Willis, with the 'berry'-shaped type being the most common. What is it?

Intracranial aneurysm: Ballooning or rupturing of a blood vessel in the brain. The risk of rupture varies with the size and location of the aneurysm, with those in the posterior circulation being more prone to rupture.
This Swiss psychologist's theory of cognitive development in children gave rise to a field he called genetic epistemology — who was he?

Also called legal theory, this field applies philosophical methods to questions like what the law is and how it ought to be — with roots traced to Confucius, Aristotle, and Enlightenment thinkers like Locke and Rousseau. What field is it?
Derived from the design of the Vought F-8 Crusader, this subsonic carrier-based light attack aircraft replaced the Douglas Skyhawk and saw extensive action in the Vietnam War — which aircraft?
LTV A-7 Corsair II: American attack aircraft family.
Used to treat everything from pneumonia to Legionnaires' disease, this broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone antibiotic is the left-handed mirror-image isomer of a drug called ofloxacin — what is it?
Levofloxacin: Antibiotic. Levofloxacin, sold under the brand name Levaquin among others, is a broad-spectrum antibiotic of the fluoroquinolone drug class.
Sometimes called the Japanese medlar or Japanese plum, this evergreen tree from the hills of south-central China produces small orange fruit — which plant?
Loquat: Species of plant. The loquat (Eriobotrya japonica, Chinese: 枇杷; Pinyin: pípá) is a large evergreen shrub or tree grown commercially for its orange coloured fruits.
Genetically related to the Bichon, Bolognese, and Havanese, this toy breed sports a silky white coat, doesn't shed, and tops out around 4 kilograms — what breed is it?
Maltese dog: Breed of toy dog. The precise link, if any, between the modern and ancient breeds is not known.
Grown from the YF-17 that lost the Air Force's lightweight fighter contest, which twin-engine carrier jet won a second life when the Navy picked it instead?
McDonnell Douglas F/A-18 Hornet: American carrier-capable multirole strike aircraft.
This British-Lebanese geometer co-founded topological K-theory and lent his name to a famous index theorem, winning both the Fields Medal and the Abel Prize — who is he?
With shovel-like front limbs built for burrowing and a mating song broadcast from a specially shaped underground tunnel, which insect is this?
Mole cricket: Members of the insect family Gryllotalpidae.
This lipid-rich substance wraps around nerve axons in segments, leaving gaps called nodes of Ranvier that let electrical signals leap along in a process called saltatory conduction — what is it?
Myelin: Fatty substance insulating nerve cell axons.
This Renaissance polymath put the Sun, not Earth, at the center of the universe in a book published just before his death in 1543 — kicking off a revolution in science. Who was he?
This soft-bodied mollusc can radically deform its shape to squeeze through tiny gaps and propels itself backward by jetting water through a siphon — what eight-limbed creature is it?
Octopus: Soft-bodied eight-limbed order of molluscs.
Also called a steer or bullock, and usually yoked in pairs, which castrated male bovine has long served as a draft animal for ploughing and hauling?
Ox: Common bovine draft and riding animal.
This Stanford biologist became famous — and controversial — for his 1968 book warning that runaway population growth would bring famine and resource depletion. Who was he?
Turning colorless in acid and a fuchsia pink in base, this phthalein dye is a favorite indicator for acid-base titrations — what is it?
Phenolphthalein: pH indicator that turns pink in basic solution.
Its name comes from the Spanish for 'little silver,' yet this dense, stubbornly unreactive metal — element 78 — is so scarce only a few hundred tonnes are mined a year. Which one?
Platinum: Chemical element with atomic number 78 (Pt)

Arising over 60 million years ago from small tree-dwellers, this order favored big brains, binocular color vision and opposable thumbs to grasp among the branches — and it includes lemurs and apes — what is it?
Primate: Order of mammals. New primate species continue to be discovered: over 25 species were described in the 2000s, 36 in the 2010s, and six in the 2020s.

Known in France as the Patou and in the US by another name, this French livestock guardian breed hails from a range straddling France and Spain, protecting flocks from wolves and bears. What breed is it?
Pyrenean Mountain Dog: French breed of dog. The Pyrenean Mountain Dog (Chien de Montagne des Pyrénées) is a French breed of livestock guardian dog.

This Canadian-American inventor pulled off the first transmission of speech by radio in 1900 and the first two-way radiotelegraphy across the Atlantic in 1906, racking up hundreds of patents — seven granted after his death. Who was this AM-radio pioneer?
Reginald Fessenden: Canadian-American electrical engineer and inventor (1866–1932)
Commonly called the dog rose, this variable climbing wild plant is native to Europe, northwest Africa, and western Asia — which species?
Also known as mucopolysaccharidosis type III, this rare genetic disorder is caused by the body's inability to break down certain sugar molecules called glycosaminoglycans — what is it called?

Sanfilippo syndrome: Rare metabolism disorder. Sanfilippo syndrome, also known as mucopolysaccharidosis type III (MPS III), is a rare lifelong genetic disease that mainly affects the brain and spinal cord.
Born in Moscow and brought to the US at age six, this computer scientist co-founded Google with Larry Page and served as president of its parent company until 2019 — who is he?
Sometimes triggered just by stepping into bright sunlight, a quirk called the photic reflex, this involuntary, explosive expulsion of air clears irritants from the nose and mouth. What is it?
Sneeze: Semi-autonomous, convulsive expulsion of air from the lungs through the nose and mouth.

Named after the patron saint of sailors, this luminous blue or violet glow appears around masts, spires, or aircraft during a strong electric field and can warn of an imminent lightning strike — what is this phenomenon called?
St. Elmo's fire: Luminous plasma created in an electric field.

Founded in 1994 and known for building nearly every component in-house, this Swedish hypercar maker set a two-way top speed record over 277 mph with its Agera RS in 2017 — what company is it?
Koenigsegg is a Swedish manufacturer of high-performance sports cars based in ngelholm, Skne County.
Its first model, the Concept One, was reportedly the world's fastest production electric vehicle with only eight ever built — which Croatian automaker is this?
Rimac Automobili (Croatian) is a Croatian automotive manufacturer headquartered in Sveta Nedelja, Croatia, that develops and produces electric sports cars.
Owned through Porsche SE by the Austrian-German Porsche-Piëch family, this Wolfsburg-based conglomerate was the largest company in the European Union in 2024 — what is it?
Volkswagen Group is a German multinational conglomerate automotive manufacturer headquartered in Wolfsburg, Lower Saxony, Germany.
Founded in 1863 as a dyestuffs partnership, this German company launched a trademarked pain reliever called Aspirin in 1899 and is headquartered in Leverkusen — which company?
Bayer: German multinational pharmaceutical and biotechnology company.
Founded in London in 1845 by an accountant of the same name, this Big Four firm is now the largest professional-services network in the world by revenue and headcount — which one?
Deloitte: Multinational professional services network. The firm was founded by the accountant William Welch Deloitte in London, England in 1845 and expanded into the United States in 1890.
Formed in 2015 when the original Hewlett-Packard split in two, this Palo Alto company kept the PC and printer business and is now the world's second-largest PC vendor behind Lenovo — which company?
HP Inc.: American information technology corporation.
Owned by Tata Motors since 2008 and granted a Royal Warrant by King George VI in 1951, this British marque now builds only upmarket four-wheel-drive SUVs — which brand?
Land Rover: Car marque and former British car company.
Founded in 1964 as "Blue Ribbon Sports" by Bill Bowerman and Phil Knight, which company later renamed itself after the Greek goddess of victory?
Nike, Inc.: American athletic equipment company.
Often called the 'forgotten founder' of Apple, this retired electronics executive partnered with Steve Wozniak and Steve Jobs to launch the company in 1976 — who is he?
Ronald Wayne: American businessperson and co-founder of Apple (born 1934)
Originally founded as Thomson-CSF in 1968 and headquartered in Paris's La Défense district, this French aerospace and defence electronics giant was rebranded in 2000 — which company?

Thales Group: French multinational company. Thales S.A., trading as Thales Group (French pronunciation: [talɛs]), is a French multinational aerospace and defence corporation specialising in electronics.
